WWE Champions·Growth diagnosis & proposal·August 2026

50 million people installed it.
The one-star reviewers
still call it fun.

Across 2,945 player reviews, the word “fun” appears at the same rate in one-star reviews as in five-star reviews. The core loop and the licence are working. What's failing is the path a new player walks in the first ten minutes — and the social layer that would have kept them. Here's what the data says, how I know it, what it's worth, and what I'd build.

The argument, in six answers

Grouped into three topics · the nine acts that follow are the evidence

The diagnosis

Evidence in Acts 01–04

01

What is the goal?

Widen the base again — don't extract harder from what's left.

A 9.5-year-old title with 50M+ installs and a 4.36★ rating has already monetised its whales close to their ceiling. The remaining upside is the players who install, look around, and leave before anything hooks them. The brief is reach and retention, not ARPPU.

02

Who is the customer?

The brand-new installer, in their first ten minutes.

Roughly 90,000 installs a month land on a three-superstar roster that already exposes a four-layer upgrade ladder, six gem stats, Trainer, Link & Gear and injury timers — and a $99.99 pack as the only item on the League 2 store shelf. The first losable match ends in a “rescue your Superstar for 100 cash” prompt.

03

Why optimise this cohort?

Because the game isn't the problem. The on-ramp is.

Across 2,945 reviews, the word “fun” appears at the same rate in 1–2★ reviews as in 4–5★ — a skew of −1.1pp. “Money” skews +26.7pp and is the most-used word in the entire corpus. Affection survives the one-star rating; what replaces it is a vocabulary of money. That is a fixable economy problem wrapped around a working loop — not a dying game.

How these three fit together

These are one chain, and the order matters. A mature live title has only two honest options — extract harder from who's left, or widen the base again — and the review corpus is what decides between them. Affection survives the one-star rating intact; what replaces it is a vocabulary of money. That rules out extraction. Widening the base then points at exactly one cohort, because the players who never survived the first ten minutes are the only group both large enough to matter and cheap enough to reach without out-bidding the casual-puzzle giants.

Each act below opens the evidence rather than restating it — the lifecycle and competitive numbers, the method and the two limits it carries, the corpus itself, and the pain points with the screenshots behind them.

The bets

Evidence in Act 05

04

What can we actually do?

Five bets. Two of them are the main event.

F1 · The Debut — defer every economy surface until the player has a roster and a win, and reveal systems on a schedule instead of dumping them. F2 · Rookie Crew — auto-draft every new player into a small social unit within minutes of install, instead of making them wait until League 5. Both raise the free-to-play floor without lowering the whale ceiling, because whales pay for relative advantage, not absolute power.

All five bets in one line each
  • 1 · The Debut. Guided first session — guaranteed marquee pull, one clear win, one next verb. 6–8 wks.
  • 2 · Rookie Crew. Social on-ramp before League 5, with a mentor and curated chat. 8–10 wks.
  • 3 · Catch-up track. Event-gated coin faucet aimed at the exact band where progression stalls. 4–6 wks.
  • 4 · Dupe protection + published odds. Duplicates convert to shards; probabilities published. 5–7 wks.
  • 5 · Tentpole win-back. Personalised reactivation timed to WrestleMania and Royal Rumble. 3–4 wks.

Act 05 · The mechanism behind each →

What they're worth

Evidence in Acts 06–07

05

Why does it matter?

Late-curve retention compounds. Early-curve retention doesn't.

On a fitted power-law curve, the D7-moving bet is worth +37% lifetime user-days per install — roughly 5× what the D1-moving bet delivers, for comparable effort. Base case for the two lead bets together: $1.3M a year, on the assumptions in Act 06. The two lead bets touch no economy surface, so they grow the base whales compete against rather than threatening revenue.

06

Which improvement ranks best?

F2 · Rookie Crew ranks first on value.
F1 · The Debut ships first.

F2 is the highest-value bet in the portfolio because it moves D7 and D30, where the curve pays. F1 ships ahead of it because it is cheaper, removes the session-one dead-ends, and feeds F2 the cohort F2 then retains. Both are gated on one week-one query: is faction-join a top-2 retention correlate? If it isn't, F2 gets re-scoped before a line of code is written.

Why value order and ship order disagree

Two different questions produce two different orders, and the proposal follows both. Value order comes from the curve: late-curve retention compounds, so F2 outranks F1 despite F1 moving the more visible metric. Ship order comes from dependency and risk: F1 is cheaper, clears the session-one dead-ends, and hands F2 a cohort worth retaining — so shipping F2 first would mean drafting players into crews they'd have quit before reaching.

Neither order survives contact with your telemetry unchanged. The ranking rests on a benchmark retention curve, and the highest-value bet rests on an assumption I inferred rather than measured. Both are the first things Act 07 goes and replaces.

01

Where this game is in its life

WWE Champions is a match-3 RPG built on one of the strongest licences in entertainment. It is also nine and a half years old and well past its growth phase. That combination decides which growth levers are worth pulling.

What that means for strategy

A mature live game has two honest options: extract harder from the players who remain, or widen the base again. The review corpus below shows what the first costs in goodwill. The second is the brief: engage more people.

That reframes the growth job. On a title this age, whales are already monetised near their ceiling. The upside is in the players who install, look around, and leave before anything has a chance to hook them — and in the social structure that turns a solo player into a committed one.

It also settles how the base gets widened. A nine-year-old match-3 title buys its installs in the same auction as the biggest casual puzzle games on the platform, against budgets it cannot match. You don't out-bid that. You out-convert it. Which puts every point of first-session retention to work twice — once as retention, and again as a cut to what an install effectively costs.

The competitive set, and one number I withdrew

Those four numbers are the lifecycle picture, and each is a direct read from a store API rather than an estimate. A game nine and a half years old, with a 50-million install base, rated 4.36, and still under active development. That is a mature title carrying a very large lapsed population and a product people demonstrably liked.

The field it's ageing in

The instinct on a licensed title is to benchmark it against the other licensed titles. That's the wrong frame, and the store data says so: nothing in wrestling is taking this game's players. The only other licensed WWE live mobile game is a card battler on a different loop; WWE 2K26 is console; AEW's mobile entry is an idle promotion-sim. The competitive set that matters is the mechanic — the match-3 collection RPGs a churned player actually opens next.

Two things fall out of that table, and neither is the one you'd expect.

  • The licence is not the problem. The other WWE game is rated 4.77 by 2.6× as many iOS raters. Wrestling fans will happily rate a WWE mobile game five stars — they're doing it next door. Whatever is costing this title goodwill, it isn't the audience or the IP.
  • The closest peer is the same age and three times the size. Empires & Puzzles launched five weeks after WWE Champions, in the same genre, with no licence at all — and carries 3.4× the iOS ratings at 4.69. Same nine years, same mechanic, no IP advantage. That is the benchmark worth studying, not SuperCard.

And the long-run comparable is MARVEL Puzzle Quest. It is the same machine — licensed characters, match-3 core, a collection ladder with an escalating top tier — launched three years earlier, and still shipping updates in 2026. It is what this structure looks like at thirteen years old.

Which makes it the most useful question in this section: where is MPQ's revenue and install curve now, relative to its peak, and does WWE Champions sit on the same line? That comparison is one paid-tool query for you and unavailable to me — and it would either validate this whole document or reframe it.

What I could not verify — and did not build on

One paywall accounts for every gap in this act. Third-party trackers are widely reported to put WWE Champions well below its 2021 peak on revenue and installs, and they publish revenue estimates for every title in the table above — putting Empires & Puzzles in the hundreds of millions a year and MARVEL Puzzle Quest far below its own peak. All of it traces back to Sensor Tower pages that need a login, and I could not open a primary source. Blog aggregations of them aren't one either.

An earlier draft of this document led with a “60% revenue decline”. I've removed it — nothing here depends on a number I can't show you. So none of the argument in this act rests on revenue at all. It rests on release dates, ratings, install counts and update cadence, which are public and re-fetchable: the comparison is structural, not financial, and the financial half is a question for someone with the licence to a data tool.

I'm flagging that rather than dropping it silently, because if the decline is real it sharpens the case considerably — and you can see the true curve in about thirty seconds. That's a question for you, not a claim from me.

02

How I looked, and what I couldn't see

No internal telemetry. So the research had to be built from what is observable — and it had to be explicit about the difference between what players say and what the data proves.

The discipline. Every claim in this document is one of three things: a verified fact, a player-reported signal, or a named gap. Player complaints are treated as hypotheses to validate against funnel and cohort data — never as measurement.

Two limits worth stating before anyone finds them. Written reviews skew negative by construction: only 8.1% of raters write text, and angry players write. And onboarding complaints are just 3% of the corpus — expected, because players who churn on day one never come back to write a review. That absence is itself the argument for pulling the funnel data.

The three methods, and the six things I'd need from you

Three methods

  • Played it. A new account to League 2, 42 screenshots of the activation window. Every claim below cites a specific screen, re-verified against the image.
  • Read it at scale. 2,945 unique reviews — 474 iOS, 2,471 Android — sampled across newest, rating and helpfulness, then de-duplicated and analysed for word frequency, theme reach, and per-rating divergence.
  • Anchored it. Google Play's full rating histogram (402,333 ratings) as the population baseline, so the review corpus is never mistaken for the player base.

What I'd need from you

  • Retention curves by lifecycle stage × spend tier — the single most important table.
  • New-user funnel, step by step: install → tutorial → first pull → first faction join.
  • ARPDAU and payer conversion by segment, to replace the benchmark assumptions in the model.
  • Gacha drop rates and pity mechanics, and whether odds have changed over time.
  • What happened around the late-2025 team-mode change — see Act 4.
03

What 2,945 players actually said

One finding reframes everything else, and it replicated independently on both platforms.

The word “fun” appears at the same rate in 1–2★ reviews (19.2%) as in 4–5★ reviews (20.3%) — a skew of −1.1 points. For comparison, “love” skews −15.0 and “money” skews +26.7. Players who rate this game one star still call it fun.

n = 2,945 · iOS + Android · the finding this whole proposal rests on

That is not what a dying game looks like. A dying game loses the loop — players stop finding it fun and say so. Here the affection survives the one-star rating intact, and what replaces it is a vocabulary of money. “Money” is the single most-used word in the entire corpus — 898 uses, ahead of “fun” at 699.

04

Five pain points, in players' own words

Each one pairs the measured signal with a verbatim review and, where I have it, a screenshot from my own first session.

The store arrives before the game does

Money lexicon · 36% of reviews · avg 2.41★

At League 2 with a three-superstar roster, the store's featured shelf holds exactly one offer — $99.99 — and the memberships tab already lists four subscriptions. Value is asked for before it is delivered.

“The game's great at getting you hooked and wanting more but the store runs more like a casino… Game's great, store is trash.” 4★ · Daniel Fulda · Play · May 2025 · 52 upvotes

The social layer is locked exactly when it's needed

Faction/social · 7% of reviews · avg 2.70★

Faction unlocks at League 5, Showdown at League 4 — the entire activation window passes without them. Meanwhile global chat is open on day one and is wall-to-wall recruitment spam and inter-faction hostility.

“Chat is often terrible. The faction quests are too hard to achieve… It's not as fun as it used to be.” 4★ · Simon Heffernan · Play · Sep 2025 · 120 upvotes

Nobody explains the game

Complexity · 3% of reviews · avg 2.37★ · under-reported by design

Four upgrade systems, six gem stats, Trainer, Link & Gear and injury timers are all exposed before a first meaningful win. Day-one churners don't write reviews, so this theme is small in the corpus and large in reality.

“No idea what I'm doing, very brief tutorials that vanish instantly… tells you you're low health but no idea what you're supposed to do about it.” 1★ · Joseph Adler · Play · Apr 2026

Progress stops without a wallet

Progress/grind · 14% of reviews · avg 2.42★

Fuse Up costs 9,000 coins and 80 shards. A three-superstar roster is gated behind 59-minute injury timers, and the fail-state offers a 100-cash rescue. Events lock behind characters you don't have.

“So many events are locked because you don't have certain characters… The game is really fun besides that.” 2★ · Chris White · Play · Feb 2025 · 231 upvotes

The odds are invisible, and trust has gone

Trust/odds · 9% of reviews · avg 2.06★ — worst of any theme

The lowest-sentiment theme in the entire corpus. Players report duplicate-heavy "guaranteed" pulls and no published probabilities, and some have organised spending bans in response.

“They claim the pulls are random but a few of us got the exact pulls… Scopely also doesn't tell you the odds.” 1★ · WhyAds · App Store · Mar 2024

Everyone wants the same fix

The most common constructive suggestion in the corpus

Players aren't asking for the economy to be dismantled. They're asking for a version of the game that a non-spender can play alongside one that a spender can dominate.

“They really need to have two or three versions of this game. They have it so geared towards whales & big spenders that the average person cannot compete.” 1★ · Scottbodin · App Store · Oct 2025
See it — the first ten minutes, in screenshots

The first ten minutes, as I experienced them

What the store promises

The current App Store listing — what a new installer is sold about thirty seconds before they meet the League 2 store.

One thing I can't explain from outside

The two most-upvoted recent Android reviews, posted a day apart in December 2025, independently say the same thing: the faction/team layer was the best part of the game, and recent changes stripped it back toward solo play.

“The game has a great faction/team element but they are now taking away all the team modes… Lots of people have left the game” — 1★, 326 upvotes. And: “Recent changes have removed most team modes… Many long time players have quit” — 1★, 55 upvotes.

If that's accurate it changes the framing of idea 2 below, and the question I'd want answered first is what the retention data showed around that change.

05

Five ideas, and the mechanism behind each

Every one raises the free-to-play floor without lowering the whale ceiling. Whales pay for relative advantage and status, not absolute power — so the two are separable, and that separation is the whole design constraint.

1

Activate · retention entry

“The Debut” — a guided first session

Defer the economy. Session one becomes a guaranteed marquee pull, one clear win, and core-loop mastery. Enhance, Fuse, Evolve, Boss Breakers and factions are revealed progressively instead of dumped at once, and the store stays shut until there's a team to spend on.

Mechanism. Cuts time-to-first-reward and removes every dead-end in session one, so more installs survive to the point where the loop can hook them.

Base-case value

6–8 wks · 1 pod
Guardrail

2

Engage · retention core

Social on-ramp before League 5

Auto-draft every new player into a small “Rookie Crew” within minutes of install, with one opt-in veteran mentor and a shared low-stakes goal. Curated chat replaces the global recruitment dump until League 4. At League 5 the crew graduates into a real faction together.

Mechanism. Faction membership is likely the strongest retention correlate in the game, and it is currently locked for the entire window in which players decide whether to stay. This moves the social tie earlier and warms the handoff instead of a cold solo join.

3

Engage · mid-game

Mid-game catch-up track

An event-gated coin-faucet and catch-up track aimed at the specific band where progression stalls — not a global giveaway. Targeted at the cohort the retention curve identifies, so it recovers churn without discounting the players who were going to pay through the wall anyway.

Mechanism. Inverts the faucet-to-sink ratio for non-payers at the stall point, converting a motivation cliff into a slope.

Monetize · trust

Dupe-protection and published odds

Duplicates convert to shards toward a star the player chooses, and pull probabilities are published. Ship to a test cohort first and read the trust and retention effect before going wide.

Mechanism. Trust is the lowest-sentiment theme in the corpus at 2.06★. Published odds are cheap to build, are already regulatory table-stakes in several markets, and directly answer the loudest constructive complaint players make.

06

What each idea is worth

A model you can audit, not a forecast. Every input is editable below — change any of them and the table recalculates. Two of them are benchmarks I'd replace with your telemetry in week one, and they're marked in red.

Open the model — every input editable

The model in one line

Fit a power-law retention curve through D1 and D7, integrate it over 180 days to get lifetime user-days per install, multiply by daily installs for steady-state DAU, and multiply by ARPDAU for revenue. A retention lift re-fits the curve; the difference in area under it is the gain. Formally: k = ln(D1/D7) / ln(7), and user-days = ∫₁¹⁸⁰ D1·d⁻ᵏ dd.

Inputs — edit any value

Assumption. Third-party estimate I could not verify at source.

Assumption. Genre range is roughly $0.15–0.40.

IdeaAssumed liftEffortΔ user-daysConservativeBase caseOptimistic
Portfolio, all five

Annualised incremental revenue. “Δ user-days” is the base-case percentage change in lifetime user-days per install — scale-invariant, so it holds regardless of whether the install and ARPDAU assumptions are right.

Read this before you read the numbers. The result is highly sensitive to the decay exponent. A ~3-point D7 lift changes lifetime user-days by roughly a third under a power-law fit, which is why idea 2 outranks idea 1 despite idea 1 moving the more visible metric.

That sensitivity is not a flaw to hide — it is the argument for measuring rather than modelling. Late-curve retention is worth more than early-curve retention on a mature title. If your real curve is flatter or steeper than the benchmark, the ranking can move, and the Δ user-days column is the part to trust: it depends only on the retention assumptions, not on the two unverified scale inputs.

Why this order

Sequenced by risk to the golden goose. Ideas 1 and 2 are retention-accretive and touch no economy surface — they grow the base whales compete against, so they help revenue rather than threaten it. Ideas 3 and 4 touch the gacha core, so they stay gated behind drop-rate and cohort-LTV data. Idea 5 is cheap and independent and can run in parallel with anything.

07

The proposal

Six data pulls to replace my assumptions, then two builds shipped as experiments with pre-agreed decision rules. Full specs follow in Act 08.

Week one — replace my assumptions

  1. Pull the cohort retention table (D1/D7/D30) by lifecycle stage × spend tier. This alone confirms or kills the ranking in Act 06.
  2. Query the new-user funnel step by step: install → tutorial → first pull → first faction join → first event complete. Find the largest single drop.
  3. Correlate “joined an active faction” and “first 4★ pull” against D7 and D30. If faction-join isn't the top retention correlate, F2 gets re-scoped before a line is written.
  4. Map faucet vs. sink per cohort to locate the stall band precisely, rather than assuming where the wall is.
  5. Pull historical free-reward tier distribution and dupe rate to confirm or refute the eroding-value hypothesis behind idea 4.
  6. Baseline DAU/MAU, sessions per day and event participation by segment — and pull retention around the late-2025 team-mode change.

Then build, in this order

PhaseWhat shipsGate to pass firstWindow
0The six pulls above; re-run the Act 06 model on real inputs—Week 1–2
1F1 · The Debut — guided first sessionFunnel data confirms a session-1 dropWeek 3–10
2F2 · Rookie Crew — social on-rampFaction-join confirmed as a top-2 retention correlateWeek 6–16
3Catch-up track and dupe-protection, in whichever order the economy data supportsF1/F2 guardrails held; drop-rate data in handWeek 17+

F1 and F2 overlap deliberately — they touch different surfaces and can be split-tested independently on the same install cohort.

What I'd want to be wrong about

  • That faction-join is the top retention correlate. It's the load-bearing assumption under the highest-value idea, and I've inferred it rather than measured it.
  • That the late-2025 team-mode change hurt. Two upvoted reviews are a signal, not a finding — the retention data around that change decides whether F2 is a restoration or a new build.
  • That the benchmark retention curve resembles yours. If your curve is materially flatter, ideas 3 and 4 move up the list.
08

The specs

Two one-pagers, written to be handed to a pod. Each states the problem, the hypothesis, what ships, what doesn't, how it's measured, and what would make us kill it.

F1 · “The Debut” — a guided first session

Ships first. Defer every economy surface until the player has a roster and a win. Primary metric D1/D7 retention of new installs; guardrail D30 payer conversion and ARPDAU, both non-inferior. Base case — a year. 6–8 weeks, one pod.

Full F1 spec — problem, flow, requirements, experiment, risks
Problem

A new player lands on a three-superstar roster that already exposes a four-layer upgrade ladder, six gem stats, Trainer, Link & Gear, Boss Breakers and injury timers. Within the first ten minutes they are offered a $99.99 pack as the only item on the League 2 store shelf, four subscription passes, and a padlocked Premium rewards column at zero points. The first losable match ends in a “RESCUE your Superstar for 100 cash” prompt.

Monetisation surfaces arrive before the player has a team, a win, or a reason to care. Nothing in the first session teaches the core loop cleanly, and several paths dead-end.

Hypothesis

If we defer every economy surface until the player has a roster and a win, and reveal systems on a schedule tied to readiness rather than dumping them at once, then time-to-first-reward falls, session-1 completion rises, and D1/D7 retention improves — without touching the economy's ceiling, because nothing about whale-facing content changes.

Goal

Primary: D1 and D7 retention of new installs.
Secondary: tutorial completion rate, time-to-first-win, time-to-first-upgrade, session-1 completion.
Guardrail: D30 payer conversion and ARPDAU, both non-inferior.

Base-case model value: +2.3% of annual revenue at the Act 06 assumptions. The honest read is that F1's value is mostly enabling — it feeds the cohort F2 then retains.

Non-goals

Not touching drop rates, pack pricing, gacha odds, or any existing player's experience. Not a tutorial rewrite for players past League 3. Not a new-art project — this reuses existing screens and changes what is shown when.

The flow

Screen 1 — the debut pull. Cold open on a named marquee superstar, granted outright. No gacha animation, no currency, no RNG. Copy frames it as a debut, not a reward. One CTA: Claim your star. Bottom-nav Store and Loot are hidden, not greyed.

Screen 2 — the first match. Match-3 plus one finisher. Boss Breakers, Link & Gear and the six gem-crit stats are suppressed. A single coach line explains the finisher bar. The match cannot be lost: if the player's health would hit zero, the opponent's next turn is scripted to miss. No rescue prompt exists in this session.

Screen 3 — the win, and one next action. Victory, XP, coins, and exactly one contextual CTA: Level up The Rock. Not six systems — one verb. Completing it fires the Level Up unlock and ends session 1 on a return hook.

Disclosure schedule

Systems unlock against triggers, one card per session, queued if they collide:

TriggerRevealsWhy there
Session 1Match-3 + finisherThe core loop, taught with one guaranteed win
First winLevel UpFirst upgrade verb — cheap, instant, satisfying
2nd match / 2★EnhanceOpens the colour-class ladder once one star exists
Day-2 return2nd superstar + teamRewards the return; introduces team-building
League 3Fuse · daily missionsDepth once a habit is forming
League 4Showdown · global chatCompetitive modes when a roster exists
League 5+Evolve · Boss Breakers · Link & Gear · crit statsEnd-game complexity for engaged players only
Requirements
  • R1. Guaranteed marquee pull fires on 100% of first sessions. No RNG on the debut pull.
  • R2. At most two systems visible in session 1; all others gated to the schedule above.
  • R3. Store, Loot, offers and subscription surfaces are hidden until the Day-2 return.
  • R4. The debut match cannot be lost, and no cash-rescue prompt can be reached in session 1.
  • R5. Every screen exposes exactly one primary CTA.
  • R6. Zero reachable dead-ends. Unavailable actions are hidden, never shown-then-blocked.
  • R7. A skip path exists for reinstalls and veterans — never trap an experienced player.
Edge cases

Interrupt or offline: resume at the last completed step, not from scratch. Reveal collision: one unlock card per session, queue the rest. Marquee already owned (reinstall with restored account): substitute the next star in the debut pool. Accessibility: coach tips dismissible, reduced-motion honoured. Skip abuse: skipping forfeits the guaranteed pull, so it can't be farmed.

Instrumentation

debut_start · marquee_claimed · first_match_win (with time_to_win) · first_upgrade_tap · system_unlock_shown and system_unlock_engaged (per system, per trigger) · dead_end_hit — must trend to zero against control · session1_complete.

All eight validated in the analytics pipeline before the experiment opens.

Experiment

Unit: new installs, 50/50 by device cohort. Control: current onboarding. Variant: The Debut.

Decision rule: ship if D7 retention clears the pre-registered MDE at p<0.05 and both revenue guardrails are non-inferior. If activation rises but D30 monetisation regresses, we bought retention by giving away the economy — hold and iterate. If guardrails hold but the primary misses, the hypothesis was wrong; say so and move to F2.

Risks

Deferred monetisation costs early revenue. Some share of players do convert on a day-1 offer. The guardrail catches it; if D30 conversion drops, we re-introduce offers earlier in the variant rather than abandoning the build.

A scripted unlosable match may read as fake. Mitigation: the assist is invisible (opponent misses), not a revive prompt. Watch qualitative feedback and session-2 return.

F2 · Rookie Crew — a social on-ramp before League 5

Highest value in the portfolio. Auto-draft every new player into a small crew within minutes of install, with a mentor and curated chat, graduating into a real faction at League 5. Primary metric share of new players in an active social unit by D7; guardrail veteran feud participation and moderation load. Base case — a year. 8–10 weeks, one pod plus moderation tooling.

Full F2 spec — problem, ladder, requirements, experiment, risks
Problem

Faction unlocks at League 5 and Showdown at League 4 — so the entire activation window passes with no social tie. Meanwhile global chat is open on day one and is wall-to-wall faction recruitment (one ad in my own session demanded “discord mandatory”) interleaved with factions insulting each other. A player is shown the party they cannot join, in the least welcoming room available, and there is no block or report tool.

Hypothesis

If a new player is placed in a small, low-stakes social unit within minutes of installing, given one shared goal and one experienced person to ask, then the share who form a social tie before they can churn rises, and D7/D30 retention rises with it — while the existing faction system is protected, because crews graduate into it rather than competing with it.

This rests on faction-join being a top retention correlate. Pull 3 in Act 07 tests that before we build.

Goal

Primary: share of new players in an active social unit by D7.
Secondary: D30 retention of crew-joiners vs. non-joiners; faction-join rate by League 5; crew-goal completion.
Guardrail: veteran feud participation, chat-report rate, moderation load.

Base-case model value: +11.7% of annual revenue — the highest of the five, because it moves late-curve retention.

Non-goals

Not replacing or re-balancing Faction Feud. Not building a new chat platform — this is a scoped channel with moderation, not a social network. Not touching veteran-facing feud scoring or rewards.

The flow

Draft. Within five minutes of install, the player is auto-assigned to a crew of four to eight, matched by install cohort and timezone so someone is actually online. Framed as being drafted, not joining a queue.

Crew home. One shared goal — a collective bar such as “win 20 matches together” — with no dead-weight penalty and none of the feud's slot requirements. A curated chat channel sits beneath it, with report and mute present from launch.

Mentor. One opt-in veteran per crew, rewarded on the crew's D7 retention rather than on their own play, so the incentive is to help rather than to farm.

Graduation. At League 5 the crew is offered a real faction together, carrying at least two crewmates where slots allow. The player arrives with people they know instead of browsing anonymous factions cold.

Social ladder
WhenSurfaceWhat it doesToday
Install +5 minRookie Crew draftAuto-assign to a cohort-matched crewNothing
Day 1Mentor matchOpt-in veteran, rewarded on crew retentionNothing
Day 1–7Crew goal + curated chatShared bar; filtered, moderated conversationUnfiltered global chat
League 4Global chat unlocksFull chat once the player can act on recruitmentOpen from day 1
League 5Graduate to FactionCrew enters a real faction togetherCold, solo join
Requirements
  • R1. Every new player is auto-assigned to a crew within 5 minutes of install.
  • R2. Crew size 4–8, matched on install cohort and timezone for live overlap.
  • R3. Curated new-player channel filters recruitment and abuse until League 4.
  • R4. Report and mute ship before the channel opens — non-negotiable.
  • R5. Mentor matching and reward loop live, and abuse-resistant (rewards on crew retention, capped per mentor).
  • R6. Graduation carries ≥2 crewmates into the same faction where slots allow.
  • R7. No crew mechanic may affect Faction Feud scoring.
Edge cases

No mentor available: crew forms anyway; the slot fills asynchronously. Crew goes inactive: auto-reshuffle stragglers into a fresh active crew rather than stranding them. Toxicity inside a crew: report and mute in-channel, with graduated enforcement. Player reaches L5 with a dissolved crew: fall back to normal faction browse. Mentor churns: reassign; never leave a crew leaderless.

Instrumentation

crew_assigned (with match-reason attributes) · crew_home_view · crew_contribution · mentor_matched / mentor_message · crew_chat_message · crew_goal_complete · graduation_to_faction (with faction_join_source) · chat_report as a moderation-health signal.

Experiment

Unit: new installs, 50/50. Control: faction at L5, global chat from day 1. Variant: Rookie Crew plus curated chat.

Decision rule: ship if D7 social-tie rate and D30 retention both lift at p<0.05 with veteran feud metrics non-inferior. The correlation that must hold: crew-joiners retain measurably better than non-joiners. If that fails, the thesis is wrong and the build stops regardless of the other numbers.

Risks

Moderation load. A new chat surface for every new player is a real cost. Mitigated by scoping the channel small, shipping tooling first, and tracking report rate as a guardrail.

Crews could cannibalise factions. Mitigated by making graduation the only exit — crews are temporary by design and cannot score in feuds.

The late-2025 team-mode change. If team modes were deliberately reduced, this build runs against a recent strategic decision. That conversation happens before the spec is approved, not after.

Sources & method

Every number in this document, where it came from, and how much weight it can carry. Anything marked Assumption is mine, not measured.

The rule I applied. Anything I could fetch and re-fetch is stated flatly. Anything computed from that data is marked reproducible and the dataset is published. Anything I could not trace to a primary source is either labelled an assumption and made editable, or removed.

The revenue decline is the one I got wrong first time round — it read well and I could not source it. It's better to lose the headline than to defend a number I can't show you.

How to reproduce this

The derived datasets are in the repository: data/review-analysis.json holds the word frequencies, divergence scores, theme reach and population histogram; data/roi-model.json holds the model inputs and per-idea outputs. The collection and analysis scripts are in scripts/. Both feeds are public and unauthenticated, so the corpus can be re-pulled and the numbers re-derived independently.
